eyebrow: 17.5 mm → 8 mm hollow conical light guide · 100 mm long · mirror wall
author_line: Hengne Li (李衡讷) · South China Normal University · Hengne.Li@cern.ch · Hengne.Li@m.scnu.edu.cn
lead: A specular ray-tracing model of this conical light guide, and a wall shape for which the simulated response map matches the measured 100×100-point scan: the two differ by {rms:.1f}% in the inner aperture, against about {noise:.1f}% single-point measurement noise. That wall is not the only one that does so. The scan fixes only a small part of the wall shape.

h_wall: A wall that reproduces the scan
p_wall:
Colour is the radial deviation δ of this wall from the ideal CAD cone. It has two parts. The azimuthal mean (panel B) says the whole bore is {mean_lo:.1f}–{mean_hi:.1f} mm narrower than CAD. The local unevenness left after removing that mean (panel A) is what creates the bright and dark structure in the response map, and its RMS is only {loc_rms:.0f} µm.

The response map is very sensitive to some shapes of unevenness. A small deformation at height z on the wall casts a thin arc of light and shade on the entrance face, and the arc moves as z changes, much as in tomography. Unevenness of order 0.03 mm is enough to change the response by a few percent.

How to read this figure: it is one wall that reproduces the scan, found by a fit that penalises unevenness and starts from an axisymmetric wall. It shows that very little unevenness is enough to explain the scan. It is not the only such wall, it is not proven to be the smoothest one, and it is not a survey of the real inner surface. The closure test below explains why.
cap_wall: The figure is vector graphics: zoom with the buttons or Ctrl + wheel, drag to pan, and hover over panel A or C to read the deviation at that point.
zoom_hint: Drag to pan, hold Ctrl and scroll to zoom
probe_idle: Hover over panel A or C for a reading
p_maps:
Putting this wall back into the ray tracer, with 40,000 rays per scan point, gives the simulated map in the middle. The off-centre dark spot, the bright ring around it and the bright patches all appear where the measurement has them. The part of the measured structure that departs from the ideal cone correlates with the simulation at {corr:.2f}.

What is left in the inner aperture is mostly point-to-point noise, plus about {excess:.1f}% of structure on a 1 mm scale that this fit does not explain (χ²/N = {chi2:.2f}). The outermost 0.4 mm ring of the aperture has larger residuals (about {rms_ring:.0f}% RMS per point, {bias_ring:+.0f}% on average). That ring was not fitted; see the limits below.
cap_maps: All three maps use scan-stage coordinates x, y. Bottom left: azimuthally averaged radial profile. Bottom right: the signal once around the ring of radius 4 mm.
step1: Measure the apertureThe edge of the scan is sharp, so the entrance centre, radius and ellipticity (about ±0.03 mm) and the light-spot size (a disc of radius about {spot_r:.2f} mm) are read off directly.
step2: Forward modelWall = CAD cone + a B-spline deviation field (24 azimuthal × 43 axial coefficients). Each source point emits Lambertian rays, they reflect specularly, and the fraction reaching the exit is counted.
step3: Linear responseAround an axisymmetric base wall, azimuthal Fourier modes of the wall are perturbed to get the effect of every coefficient on the map: the Jacobian.
step4: Iterative inversionDamped least squares with a smoothness penalty. Every trial step is checked with a full ray trace, and the iteration stops when no trial step lowers the objective any more.
p_method:
The inversion rests on a clean property of the ideal cone: for a diffuse source the transmission averaged over the entrance equals (Rout/Rin)² = 20.9% exactly (conservation of étendue), and from point to point it changes by only +{centre_dev:.2f}% at the centre to −{rim_dev:.2f}% at the rim. The several-percent structure in the measured map therefore cannot come from an ideal cone. In this model it is attributed to the wall departing from the ideal shape.

The fit uses a purpose-written tracer rather than Geant4: one inversion traces of order 1011 rays while the wall shape keeps changing. The tracing kernel runs in OpenCL on this machine's Radeon 8060S at tens of millions of rays per second, roughly an order of magnitude faster than the CPU version on all cores. Geant4 serves as the independent check.
h_check: How far the result can be trusted
p_check: The checks below answer three different questions: is the tracer right, can the inversion recover a known answer, and how much does the result depend on the assumptions. The first group passes. The closure test shows where the method stops.
earlier: (Result of an earlier run, not repeated for this wall.)
row_g4ideal_n: Geant4 (G4Cons) at {npoints} source points along a radius, {nphot} photons each; ratio to the tracer {ratio:.4f} ± {ratio_err:.4f}. The area ratio (R<sub>out</sub>/R<sub>in</sub>)² is 0.2090
row_g4wall_n: The wall was turned into a cavity of 720,000 triangular facets and recomputed with Geant4 optical photons, {npoints} source points × {nphot} photons, with the light spot and mirror of the fit. Normalised point-by-point scatter {pull_rms:.2f} (1 means pure statistics)
row_gpu_n: Same wall and same rays at {npoints} source points × {nray} rays. In double precision the GPU reproduces the CPU transmission of every point to rounding error. In single precision, which the fit uses, the mean relative difference is {mean} ± {err} and the point-to-point scatter {rms}
row_recip_n: The flux from entrance to exit must equal the flux the other way. A wrong intersection or surface normal breaks this identity
row_closure_n: Known wall (7 bumps and dents) → noisy synthetic scan → same pipeline, given the entrance aperture of that wall. The synthetic scan is fitted down to the noise (χ²/N = {chi2:.2f}), so the pipeline reaches the noise level when the model is right
row_closure2_n: The recovered wall is only weakly correlated with the true one: true local unevenness {rms_true:.0f} µm RMS, recovered {rms_rec:.0f} µm, and the azimuthal mean profile is off by {prof_err:.0f} µm RMS.
row_closure2_res: Inside the 30 shape patterns the scan determines best, recovered and true wall correlate at {c30:.2f}; inside the best 100 at {c100:.2f}, inside the best 150 at {c150:.2f}. These hold {f30:.0f}%, {f100:.0f}% and {f150:.0f}% of the true deformation. The transition is gradual, not a sharp cut-off
row_prev_k: Two fits of the measured scan
row_prev_n: The wall published before the tracer corrections, traced with the present tracer, still reproduces the scan to {rms_earlier:.2f}%, against {rms_now:.2f}% for the present wall; the two simulated maps differ by {map_diff:.2f}%. Yet the two walls are different: their local unevenness correlates at {corr_local:.2f} over the whole wall ({corr_entrance:.2f} in the first 20 mm behind the entrance, none further in), and their azimuthal mean profiles are {prof_diff:.0f} µm RMS apart, up to {prof_diff_max:.0f} µm. This is the non-uniqueness, seen directly on the measured data
row_jac_n: Random smooth non-axisymmetric deformations of 10–100 µm RMS, around the base wall and around the fitted wall: the linear prediction of the change of the map correlates with the exact change at {corr_min:.2f}–{corr_max:.2f}, with a slope of {slope_min:.2f}–{slope_max:.2f}. Axisymmetric changes are predicted poorly: correlation {m0_smooth_corr_min:.2f}–{m0_smooth_corr_max:.2f} for a gentle bump 30 µm high, {m0_step_corr_min:.2f}–{m0_step_corr_max:.2f} for a sharp 50 µm step. Every step of the fit is therefore accepted only after a full ray trace
row_refl_n: Starting from the perfect-mirror fit and freeing the mirror reflectivity, the axisymmetric fit moves to R = {refl:.2f}; χ² falls from {chi2_fixed:.0f} to {chi2:.0f} ({npts} points, one more parameter) and the wall profile changes shape but keeps its size. Reflectivity and profile are strongly degenerate, this scan cannot separate them, and the result is quoted for a perfect mirror
cap_closure: Closure test. Left: the true local unevenness put in. Middle: what the inversion recovers from the synthetic scan (same colour scale). Right: azimuthal mean profile. The two walls give the same response map within the noise.
cav1: The solution is not uniqueDifferent walls give the same response map within the noise. Two fits of the measured scan reproduce it equally well with walls that agree only close to the entrance (correlation {prev_corr_local:.2f} overall). In the closure test the true wall is recovered well only inside the roughly 100 shape combinations the scan determines best (correlation {resolution_c100:.2f}), and these hold {resolution_f100:.0f}% of the true deformation: the trace of broad, gentle bumps 0.15–0.3 mm high is equally produced by a much smoother wall. Shown here is one regularised solution. The fit penalises unevenness and starts from an axisymmetric wall, so it tends to a smooth wall, but nothing proves it is the smoothest wall that fits.
cav2: The azimuthal mean profile is poorly fixedIt is strongly degenerate with the overall signal scale, the exit radius and the mirror reflectivity, and different fits return different profiles: the present one and the one published before the tracer corrections are {prev_prof_diff:.0f} µm RMS apart (up to {prev_prof_diff_max:.0f} µm), and in the closure test the recovered profile is off by {closure_prof_err:.0f} µm RMS. Common to all fits are only the entrance radius (measured directly) and a bore narrower than CAD along the whole length. The local unevenness is {loc_rms:.1f} µm RMS here and {prev_loc_rms_earlier:.1f} µm in that earlier wall; a still earlier fit from another starting point gave 44 µm. All reproduce the scan to about 1%. The linear response used by the fit is itself weak in this direction: a smooth deformation is the small remainder of large, cancelling responses of single spline knots, and for a gentle axisymmetric bump the kernel predicts the pattern of the change with a correlation of only {jacobian_m0_smooth_corr_min:.2f}–{jacobian_m0_smooth_corr_max:.2f}. Steps along the mean profile are found inefficiently, and the resolution figures of the closure test, which rest on the same kernel, are only indicative for broad smooth shapes.
cav3: Everything is blamed on geometryBy assumption the mirror reflectivity is 1, the PMT is uniform and the source is an ideal Lambertian. Real reflectivity variations, the seam of the reflective film or photocathode non-uniformity would all be read as wall unevenness.
cav4: The entrance rimBetween r = 8.0 mm and the aperture edge ({r_ap:.2f} mm) the measurement lies below the model: by {ring_low:.1f}% of the plateau on average over the ring from 8.0 to 8.5 mm, and by {ring_low_worst:.1f}% in the worst 0.1 mm annulus. The measurement drops earlier than the model inside the aperture but shows no tail outside, as if a band about 0.1 mm wide at the rim were lossy (a chamfer, or film that stops short of the edge). This is below the model resolution and was not fitted.
cav5: What would pin down the real wallIndependent information: scans with a collimated beam at several incidence angles, angle-resolved readout at the exit, a scan from the exit side, or direct profilometry of the wall. Each new measurement constrains a further set of shape combinations.
cav6: Orientation of the azimuthφ is defined by the scan x and y. Relating it to the hardware needs the orientation of the stage axes with respect to the light guide, and which of the 4 cells was scanned.
cav7: The fit is not a proven optimumχ²/N is {chi2:.2f}, not 1, and about {excess:.1f}% of structure remains. The iteration stops when no trial step improves the fit. That does not prove that no better wall exists, nor that the remaining structure is beyond a smooth mirror wall: earlier fits of the same scan, with earlier versions of the code, stopped at χ²/N of 1.48 and 1.31.
p_files: The code is a stand-alone toolkit, LGWallRecon: the tracer (CPU and GPU), the inversion pipeline, the closure test, the Geant4 check and user manuals in Chinese and English.

f3_title: Closure test: how well is a known wall recovered?

f3_foot: Both walls give the same response map within the noise (residual {map_rms:.2f}%), yet the walls correlate at only {corr_all:.2f}: true unevenness {rms_true:.0f} µm, recovered {rms_rec:.0f} µm. The scan does not determine the wall uniquely.
